correctness.rationale: The 20-vertex Folkman graph and all degree-four updates are given by explicit incidence equations. Exhaustive finite successor-graph traversal classifies each of 2^20 states, giving the 12 exact nonzero first-entry/period populations. A separate NumPy bit-sliced implementation derives those populations independently by testing F^(t+2)=F^t for t=0,...,7, with no unclassified states and exact witnessed sharp time seven. The 960 maximal-delay states all reach unanimity (480 of each colour). The complete 3840-element automorphism group follows from five duplicate-neighborhood vertex pairs; generator traversal yields 44 fixed-state and eight two-cycle space-time classes, whose component populations sum exactly to 4036 and 702. C++ source, independent checker, outputs and witness are provided in this same package.

originality.rationale: This claim concerns the complete first-entry-time and temporal-period table and complete symmetry quotient on the specific 20-vertex Folkman graph. The complete inspected 2015 preprint on deterministic majority proves general eventual two-periodicity and graph contraction bounds, but gives neither the exact Folkman counts nor its sharp seven-step tail. Closest indexed finite majority censuses concern nonisomorphic McGee, Nauru, Heawood, four-cube, Tutte-Coxeter and other graphs; none implies the claimed Folkman-specific integer table. value.rationale: The smallest semisymmetric graph is a canonical natural benchmark for symmetry-sensitive threshold dynamics because its 20 vertices occupy two fundamentally inequivalent graph orbits. Exact 44/8 recurrent symmetry classes and a consensus-only seven-step tail describe the full discrete phase portrait, rather than a chosen small subfamily or routine parameter variation. The sharp separation between oscillatory basin entry at t<=3 and fixed-state entry up to t=7 is not implied by eventual period-two theory and can test voting-time symmetry reductions. The exact invariant is valuable as a complete benchmark without a claimed broader family theorem.
